cells.tense: Right now the books between you and the people close to you are open and honest.
cells.ask: Text one person thanks for one specific thing, no apology, no offer of anything back.
cells.core:
You're keeping the books level without needing a ledger. There's a tab running in your head for the people close to you, and right now it reads fair — what you give and what you take land even. You can tell when you're owed a little, you can tell when you owe, and you can wait without writing it down.

This is what you built after some hard ending or other. Things that change don't have to take the fairness with them. You forget it's working because it's quiet — nothing tips, nobody gets a bill. What holds the friendship steady is that you let it be level, not that you keep checking. One thing it costs to keep: letting someone stay a little in your debt without reaching to settle it. Today, leave one exchange open and let it be.
cells.sheetLine: You keep things even and let them stay even.
cells.verb: balancing what passes between you, one exchange at a time
cells.place: in the living room of what's shared between you and the people close to you

cells.tense: You're bracing for a bill that hasn't been written yet, settling accounts before anyone has spent anything.
cells.ask: For one day, don't bring up money owed or favours owed to anyone. Let every debt sit.
cells.core:
You're standing at the register when nobody else has walked up. Somewhere ahead of you is a version where the exchange goes wrong, where you've given more than you got back, and you're already there — settling, evening, keeping score before the score exists. Fairness has turned into arithmetic you run at night.

What that arithmetic costs is the exchange itself. Friendships get held up to the light and weighed, and the weighing is starting to be the relationship. You can stay steady through hard times without turning every kindness into a line item. The books are not actually what holds these people to you. Today, do nothing about the debts. Notice how much room there is when you stop balancing.

cells.tense: There's a door you stopped walking through, and the people are on the other side of it.
cells.ask: Ask one person for a favour before you've decided whether you'll need it.
cells.core:
You show up and you keep things going, but you stand just outside the exchange now. Close enough to hand things over, not quite in it yourself. You carry alone what other people would have happily halved, and you call it being fine.

What's thin here isn't kindness — you've got plenty of that. It's the receiving, and the asking that comes before it. Start smaller than the people. One want named quietly to yourself, one careful judgment made and kept, and then another. That steadiness is what makes the asking possible. Loosen the grip on one want today. Ask for the small thing, plainly, no apology built in.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped taking your half of what's shared.

cells.tense: The give and take is already running between you, and you would say you don't do fairness.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, one thing you want kept fair between you and someone, before you decide it's worth it.
cells.core:
You'd say you don't keep score. But when someone takes more than their share, something in you writes it down — you just haven't been saying so. You're holding the exchange steady, generous where it's needed, patient where it's slow, and calling it not a big deal, or that's just how they are. The pacing other people feel from you is this; you just don't claim it as yours.

What you know about it is already there before you argue the case. The sense of what's fair lands first — usually right, usually quiet, and then a step behind it the explaining starts. Let one piece of that land without the explaining after it. One thing you've wanted kept even, said once, before you've checked whether it sounds reasonable.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping it even while saying you're not counting.

attempts.check: The draft's weakest claim is that the person must 'name the fairness' in the Unacknowledged cell; the record supports that recounting is running, but not that the person has never spoken it. A reader could say 'I already named that, nothing changed' — so the ask points at one thing kept off the list, not at a first confession. If the read is wrong, the ask still gets a plain account into daylight, which is useful on its own. The sentence serving the writer more than the person would be any claim that the accounting was hidden; the cells below keep to what can be seen — the adding, the writing-ahead, the door, the untallied cost.
